title: Distributed job scheduler
summary: Run one-off and cron jobs on time on a shared worker fleet: 10M runs a day, 50,000 of them due in the same second at the top of each hour, each run at least once and never silently lost.
interviewerPrompt: Our teams run thousands of cron jobs on their own servers and keep missing runs when a box dies. Design a shared job scheduler they can all use instead. Jobs should run on time and must not get lost.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What kinds of schedules?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One-off jobs at a given time ('run this at 18:00 tomorrow') and recurring jobs with cron expressions, each with a time zone. One-off jobs can also be submitted to run as soon as possible.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many runs?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 10M executions a day from 5,000 internal owners. Roughly 70% come from recurring schedules and 30% are one-off submissions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the load spread evenly?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Many cron schedules fire at minute 0 of every hour, so the top of each hour is a sharp peak; midnight UTC is the worst, when daily jobs fire on top of the hourly ones.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How punctual must a run be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A run should start executing on a worker within 5 s of its scheduled time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does a job actually do, and how long does it take?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It is a container image and command run on our shared worker fleet. Runs take from a few seconds to an hour; most are short.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Exactly once or at least once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At least once: a scheduled run must never be silently skipped, and failed runs are retried. Owners accept that a run may occasionally execute twice, but want to know how to make that harmless.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should happen if a run is still going when the next one is due?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The owner chooses per job: allow overlap, skip the new run, or cancel the old one and start the new one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What do owners need to see?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Every run's status, timings, attempt history, exit code and logs, through a UI and an API. They also want an alert when their job fails or does not run.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do jobs depend on each other?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not in this version. Workflows and DAGs between jobs are out of scope; a job can submit another one-off job through the API.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we manage the worker machines?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the shared fleet is ours, and it can be scaled up and down; new worker hosts take a minute or two to become ready.

deepDiveQuestions: How do you store job definitions and turn cron schedules into on-time triggers without scanning every job every second?
Who fires a due job: a single leader or partitioned schedulers, and how do you stop two schedulers firing the same run?
How do you guarantee at-least-once execution, and what must job owners do to make a second run harmless?
How do retries, timeouts and overlapping runs work, and how do you absorb 50,000 jobs due in the same second?
How do owners see what happened to every run, and how do you know the scheduler itself is running late?

runChallenge.title: Midnight burst with a zone down
runChallenge.description: Run the midnight burst (2× an ordinary hour mark: 20,000 runs fired per second, 28,800 worker reports per second) and lose the busiest availability zone after 10 s. Firing and worker reports must keep up with under 0.5% errors and a p99 under 200 ms, with no single point of failure.

commonMistakes: Polling the whole jobs table every second for due jobs, which works with a thousand jobs and melts the database at a million.
Sizing from the daily average of about 116 runs a second when 50,000 runs are due in the same second at the top of every hour.
Promising exactly-once execution. A worker can finish the job and die before reporting success; the honest guarantee is at-least-once plus idempotent jobs.
Using a distributed lock or leader lease as the only guard against double firing, with no fencing token or unique run key, so a paused scheduler fires again when it wakes up.
Running jobs with no lease or heartbeat, so a run on a dead worker stays 'running' forever and is never retried.
Retrying immediately and indefinitely, turning one failing downstream dependency into a retry storm, with no dead-letter state for runs that will never succeed.
Storing next-run times in local time without a daylight-saving policy, so a 02:30 job runs twice or never on clock-change nights.
Having no way to detect that the scheduler itself is late or down: a scheduler that silently stops looks exactly like a quiet night.
